newsitem.title: KENYA: Security blanket to avert Nairobi Budget Day protest.
newsitem.headline: Security blanket to avert Nairobi Budget Day protest.

text.p: The Kenyan government threw a thick security blanket over central Nairobi on Thursday to prevent an opposition protest at parliament on Budget day.
Hundreds of police backed by the feared anti-riot General Service Unit (GSU) deployed at strategic points in and around the capital.
Armed with long wooden staves, shields and teargas canisters, they sealed off the parliament building.

The normally bustling city centre was semi-deserted all day. Shops as well as some schools and offices were closed with people fearing a violent confrontation between the security forces and activists demanding sweeping constitutional reforms before elections.
Shopkeepers, many of whom are of Indian and Pakistani descent, feared a repeat of two days of looting after an opposition rally was forcibly dispersed by police on May 31.
"We are closing early because we are scared," shop owner Megufa Delve told Reuters.
"We are going to close today because of total insecurity. We have moved all goods from display windows already," said Japrakash Mishra of retail chain Nakumatt.
Reform leaders under the coalition National Convention Assembly banner (NCA) said earlier they would give members of parliament copies of two constitutional reform bills.
But Willy Mutunga, a leading NCA member, told Reuters the heavy security had forced a change of plan.
"Our strategy was to assemble outside parliament. This is not going to be possible because there is a lot of security.
"The action is going to be within parliament itself. We hope that members of parliament will get inside and not just disrupt but insist that the (NCA-sponsored) bills are debated," Mutunga said.

Police cleared civilians for a radius of several hundred metres (yards) when President Daniel arap Moi arrived at parliament to hear Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi's 1997/98 budget speech. The scheduled 2.30 p.m. (1130 GMT) start of the speech was delayed.
Police armed with rifles manned roadblocks on access roads into Nairobi.
City centre banks remained open and the shilling was stable. Business on the Nairobi Stock Exchange was sluggish with some brokers closing 15 minutes early.
Some staff at the downtown U.S. embassy stayed away from work, heeding advice not to come if they feared trouble.
Staff worked normally at the giant U.N. complex at Gigiri, 10 km (six miles) from the city centre.
"We are working normally but staff have been advised to be cautious and to try to avoid the city centre on Thursday," U.N. spokesman Tore Brevik said.
"It is clear that we may be entering an unsettled period," the headmaster of one suburban private school wrote in a letter to parents.
"I feel, in the interests of safety, it is best to take a low profile and reduce travelling to a minimum," he added, cancelling a school trip to Nairobi's museum on Thursday.
Moi has agreed to relax a tough law restricting public assemblies but ruled out any more constitutional reforms until after general elections to be held this year.

Moi, 73 this year, has yet to announce the election date. He looks certain to extend his 19-year rule for another five years, both because of the existing electoral rules and the deep personal and ethnic splits within the opposition.
A Western diplomat said the government was set to announce a concession by extending the registration of voters nationwide by two weeks from the original deadline of June 22.
The National Electoral Commission said on Wednesday it had so far registered only 5.1 million voters, half the estimated electorate in the country of nearly 30 million.
Despite the ban on the opposition rally, hundreds of supporters of Moi's ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) were allowed to gather in central Nairobi, chanting praises for the government.
Some told reporters they had been paid by Kanu to disrupt the NCA march to parliament.
"We do not need a permit to march because we are on the side of KANU. We are working with the police and we are ready to disrupt the opposition march," KANU official Joseph Nyakunde said.
